requirements.nl_text: Request Number - 328 | Request Title - Feature request: Sending dummy short messages | Request Description - TextSecure could mask meaningful communication between people by occasionally sending dummy random messages to random recipients at random times:  Recipients would be chosen randomly between contacts that knowingly use TextSecure, so it could be recognized as such after decryption and automatically discarded by recipient. "Randomness" should be tweaked to level-out the legitimate messages, spoiling the traffic analysis of traffic retention data, preventing to weigh connections in the deducted social network graph or guessing sleeping/activity patterns. People often have many unused messages in their monthly quota, so those could easily be used with no extra cost, or they value their privacy more than some money. Sender would need to enable this feature (opt-in) and define desired quantity (eg max 100 dummy messages per month, 2 dummy messages for every legitimate one, max 500 messages total counting legitimate and dummy ones...). The feature would need to be aware of roaming (disabled by default, optionally enable) and battery level (do not send if bellow eg. 30%). http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_analysis#Countermeasures Possible extensions:  Recipients could be able to let their peers know, that they do not want to participate in this and do not want to receive messages for whatever reason (opt-out). Recipients could also be chosen randomly between other contacts (those not using TextSecure yet) to promote its use (default message) or a custom explanation by sender. Those messages would be in clear text. As this might be annoying it should be very limited (eg max 1 message to a single recipient per month, only during daytime...) to not be too intrusive spam. Dummy messages could contain other peer's phone numbers (random selection from those participating in dummy messaging, not just their contacts), never to be shown to user, just to send dummy messages to, to further mask the real social network. It would be tricky to opt-out later on once your number starts circulating, so opt-outs would need to be spread this way as well and by direct reply dummy message or by defining a TTL of each such number.

verdict.text:
Track 1 cannot answer the fabrication question on this run, even though support is non-zero. The 56 "silently filled" slots are all scope (42) and condition (14). The model's outputs suggest these are not invented content but simple omission. In 222-Signal#1 and the whole 802 cluster, the LLM writes "<MISSING_ACTOR> <MISSING_MODAL_VERB> export the "public keys" to a "file"". There is no scope or condition text at all, only an absent placeholder. The human annotators instead write explicit "<MISSING_SCOPE>, <MISSING_CONDITION>," prefixes. The scorer appears to classify an absent placeholder as "filled", so a 0.0 flag rate measures the zero-shot prompt's output format, not fabrication. This should be confirmed against the raw outputs before anything is reported. Scope and condition are also optional in Rimay, and the gold marks all 42 requirements as complete, so their absence was never a defect. For the obligatory slots (actor, modalVerb, action), gold-missing support is zero, so fabrication of core content is simply not testable on this subset.

What the data does show is the opposite of the feared failure mode. Where humans treated actor and modal verb as implied and wrote "the App must let the user…", the model refused to infer them. It emitted MISSING_ACTOR in 15 cases and MISSING_MODAL_VERB in 29. This is over-conservatism, and it drives the 0.19 completeness agreement: 34 of 42 outputs were declared incomplete against a gold that called every one complete. Whether that counts as an error depends on a study-design decision you have not yet made: is inferring "the App" as actor legitimate implication or fabrication? The humans say implication.

On similarity, the LLM sits clearly below the human ceiling on every measure. Sequence ratio is 0.60 versus 0.79, cosine 0.76 versus 0.89, and Jaccard 0.45 versus 0.61. However, the worst examples show the action content is nearly identical to the humans'. 802-Signal#3, #4 and #6 match the annotators almost word for word after the prefix. Much of the gap is therefore template boilerplate: the humans share a long common prefix that inflates their agreement, and the LLM uses a different placeholder scheme. The 0.15–0.19 gap is real, but it mostly reflects format divergence rather than semantic disagreement.

Paska largely re-detects the model's own placeholders rather than providing independent evidence. "Modal verb is missing in the SR" fires wherever the model emitted MISSING_MODAL_VERB. "Not requirement" fires on all 13 cases where both actor and modal verb were placeholders, which covers the entire 802 cluster plus 222-Signal#1, 226 and 6362#1–2. The perfect pass rate for llm_complete outputs (8/8) versus 5/34 is the same fact counted twice. The genuinely stylistic findings are few. There is passive voice in conditions for 6390-Signal#1 and #2, and actors missing from conditions for 222-Signal#2 and #3. That is four instances, too few to characterise.

The sample is small and heavily clustered. The 42 units come from about 14 source requests, and units from one request behave identically: all six 802 units fail the same way. The effective sample size is therefore closer to 14 than 42, and differences of a few points between strategies will be noise. As the brief notes, this is also the pre-filtered atomic subset, so none of this generalises to unfiltered feature requests.

The most useful next step is to fix the measurement before comparing strategies. First, check how the scorer labels absent scope and condition placeholders, and either make the prompt emit them explicitly or score absence as "missing". Second, decide and document whether "the App" counts as implied or fabricated, and align the prompt with that convention. Third, recompute similarity on the action segment alone so that template differences stop masking content agreement. Until those changes are made, comparing zsl against fsl or cot on these metrics would mostly compare output formats.
